The [performance card](https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html) measures this on NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3, a million samples integrated for up to 1000 steps.

On a batch where samples finish at different times:

- the compacted graph takes 16 ms, against 2.13 ms for the identical workload run without compaction — at this size compaction costs more than it saves;
- an occasional physical reorder layered on top, opt-in and triggered only once the live samples have thinned and scattered, cuts that further to 10.7 ms;
- `eagle.simulate` — the policy that picks between these approaches at run time, so nobody has to choose by hand — reaches 613 µs on this same batch, ahead of NVIDIA Warp (1.54 ms), JAX (47 ms), CuPy (368 ms) and PyTorch with torch.compile (84.5 ms) on this card.

On a batch where every sample runs the full 1000 steps instead, there is nothing to compact, and the plain graph is the better fit: 2.32 ms against 22.9 ms for the compacted graph, whose periodic active-set scan runs with no idle lanes left to recover. NVIDIA Warp's per-thread kernel and `eagle.simulate` tie here (1.71 ms and 1.75 ms), and at N = 10,000 `eagle.simulate` leads (112 µs against 121 µs) — worth knowing about. The card also lists the regimes where another approach is the better fit: the same computation written as masked CuPy array code is the better fit when array-style code matters more than wall time.
